title_original: Stephen Shore: “The World Would Be a Better Place if Everyone Really Paid Attention”
excerpt_original: In The Mental Image, Stephen Shore finally puts into words a tradition he has carried privately for forty years – that a photograph can hold the trace of a mind, not just a scene. L’article Stephen Shore: “The World Would Be a Better Place if Everyone Really Paid Attention” est…

blocks.text: The desert at Big Bend National Park does not give a photographer much to hold onto: no trees to break the horizon, no telephone poles to organise the eye, nothing but heat rising off dry ground and a sky as cloudless as a wall. It was here, in 1987, that Stephen Shore set up his 8×10 camera and made two photographs of the same landscape, under the same light and at the same exposure. Nothing in the scene had changed. What changed was what Shore was seeing. In one photograph, he held the horizon in his mind as a flat line; in the other, he concentrated on its depth – the sheer distance folding out toward the vanishing point. The camera had not moved, yet experienced photographers could see a difference between the two images. What, exactly, had happened between those exposures, in the emptiest of landscapes, where nothing changed but the photographer’s mind?

Since American Surfaces and Uncommon Places , Shore has made a practice of looking at the ordinary until it becomes newly strange. While writing The Nature of Photographs , he hesitated to describe the tradition behind this way of seeing. Now, approaching seventy-nine, he has decided to take the risk. “I don’t care if people think it’s a little off the wall,” he says.

blocks.alt: Contact sheet of 16 colour frames of houses, streets and a flowered armchair in Durango, Colorado, photographed in July 1972 for American Surfaces
blocks.caption: Stephen Shore, contact sheet from American Surfaces, Durango, Colorado, 1972, from The Mental Image (MACK, 2026). Courtesy of the artist and MACK.

blocks.text: The tradition he describes is not so much a school of thought as a thread running quietly through American photography – from Stieglitz and Weston through Adams, Minor White, Paul Caponigro and Frederick Sommer. Weston called it “previsualizing,” but Shore is interested in what might happen before the shutter: in the photographer’s awareness of seeing photographically, and in the possibility that this awareness itself leaves a trace.

After Big Bend, Shore called Sommer, who told him he understood what had happened. “Minor White thinks it’s mystical, but it’s physics,” he said. That idea lingers through the book. Shore does not know what the physics might be; he points instead to the interstitial system – a network of fluid-filled spaces in the body – as an example of something physical that may exist before we have the language to describe it. “I’m not going to pretend I understand how this works,” he says. Asked whether he can see the difference himself, his answer comes without hesitation: yes.

Then the past unexpectedly supplied its own evidence. About two weeks after Shore repeated the experiment with a student, photographing the same brick wall under identical conditions, Eleanor Caponigro sent him a story about the composer Ernest Bloch and Stieglitz. In 1917, Bloch challenged Stieglitz’s claim that photography was an art. Stieglitz invited him to the studio, and they made exactly the same picture. That evening, in the red darkroom light, they processed their prints in the same tray and watched the images rise from the blank paper, side by side. Bloch could see immediately. His was “dull and drab”; Stieglitz’s was “alive.” Shore realised that the experiment he had just performed had already unfolded once before, nearly a century earlier. The coincidence feels almost like another experiment – evidence arriving from the past.

blocks.text: The Mental Image is full of attempts to give physical form to what usually remains invisible: the moment when an intention becomes a choice, when looking becomes seeing, when experience enters the photograph. But Shore is careful about the limits of what he knows. The effect, he argues, depends on fluency – on spending enough time with a camera and the materials of photography that thought becomes embodied. He compares it to a basketball player imagining a free throw: visualisation matters because the body already knows what it is being asked to do. “Some of the exercises in the book only work once there’s a foundation of real technical material and formal experience,” he says.

The view camera makes this argument physical: heavy, slow and demanding. Shore places a coin on the ground to mark the tripod’s exact position before walking back to retrieve the camera; when he returns, the tiny marker allows him to reconstruct it. The camera weighs around seven kilograms; setting it up means moving through a sequence of physical decisions before the picture can exist. “Every decision becomes physical,” Shore says. The camera does not disappear into photographing; it makes the act impossible to ignore.

blocks.text: Shore has spent more than forty years teaching, trying to slow the interval between looking and making. In the early 1970s, he would stop at random moments and become conscious of what he was seeing, making what he now calls a “screenshot of [his] field of vision.” Later, he walked through New York without a camera, watching visual relationships change as he moved. The point was not simply to find pictures, but to cultivate a way of being in the world. He wanted to capture, he says, “not just the scene, but the act of paying attention, and what it looks like to pay attention.”

It is an idea that lands differently now, when a photograph can be made before the decision to make it has registered. The phone can slip between seeing and thinking; the view camera, by contrast, keeps the apparatus in the body’s awareness. He can stand beside it, register the wind, the light, a shift in someone’s expression. The experience, he says, is deeper – yet he is wary of doctrine. “I’m not writing a prescription,” he says. His hope as a teacher is more modest, but possibly more radical: to help students “see the world with attention.” He extends the thought beyond photography. “I think the world would be a better place if everyone really paid attention.”

blocks.alt: Open book spread of The Mental Image: a colour photograph of Tanya Marcuse's Fallen No. 45, withered apples among leaves and moss, facing a page of text on attention and childhood experience
blocks.caption: Book spread from The Mental Image (MACK, 2026) by Stephen Shore. Courtesy of the artist and MACK.

blocks.text: Shore does not claim to have discovered a mechanism at Big Bend, only an experience difficult to explain. Perhaps that is the point. The photograph may contain no visible record of the thought that made it, yet something of that thought remains: a trace between the world and the picture, between seeing and photographing, between what can be explained and what can only be noticed. That small gap is where The Mental Image lives. Shore does not close it. He gives it a name.
The Mental Image (2026) by Stephen Shore is published by MACK and available for £20.
